title: Expressions with other common verbs
subtitle: look into, run out of, turn up, let slip, break off
summary: Learn common expressions built on the everyday verbs look, see, run, turn, let and break, and use them naturally in sentences.

lesson.heading: Look
lesson.text: **Look** combines with particles to make a whole family of expressions. Notice that **look down on** and **look up to** are exact opposites, and that **look into** and **look at** are close but not identical: you **look into** a problem to investigate it, and you **look at** the evidence to examine it.

examples.text: I **look forward to** hearing from you at your earliest convenience.
examples.note: used at the end of a formal letter

examples.text: The police are **looking into** the matter.
They need to **look at** all the evidence before reaching a decision.
She **looks down on** anyone she thinks is inferior to her.
examples.note: looks down on = despises; the opposite is look up to = admire

examples.text: It's hard to be positive but do try to **look on the bright side**.
examples.note: look on the bright side = be optimistic

lesson.heading: See
lesson.text: **See about** and **see to** both mean to deal with something practical. **See someone off** is what you do at a station or airport, and if you **see through** a person you realise they are trying to deceive you.

examples.text: Sue tries to **see about** arrangements for the conference at least a year ahead.
examples.note: see about / see to = deal with

examples.text: We all went to **see** Jana **off** at the airport.
It didn't take Tom long to **see through** her.
examples.note: understand that she was trying to deceive him

examples.text: That can't be Hamid. He's in Paris this week. I must be **seeing things**.

lesson.heading: Run
lesson.text: Something that **runs out** comes to an end; you **run out of** the thing itself. If you **run into** someone you meet them by chance, and **in the long run** means in the distant future rather than right now.

examples.text: I **ran into** an old friend yesterday - I had no idea she was in town.
Her patience has **run out** and she has told him she won't help him any more.
We've **run out of** milk.
Let's **run over** the plans again to make sure we've thought of everything.
Things may be hard now but it'll be worth it **in the long run**.
The trains have stopped **running** because of the avalanche.

lesson.heading: Turn
lesson.text: **Turn down** means reject, **turn up** means appear (often unexpectedly), and something that **turns out to be** X is discovered to be X. **Turn over a new leaf** means to start behaving in a better way.

examples.text: Everyone was very surprised when she **turned down** the promotion and explained that she was leaving the company.
Naoko **turned up** last night. I haven't seen her for years!
I'm going to **turn over a new leaf** this year and answer all my letters the day I get them!
The fire bell **turned out to be** a false alarm.

lesson.heading: Let
lesson.text: If someone **lets you down** they disappoint you by not doing what they promised. **Let go of** something is to stop holding it. A court **lets someone off** with a small punishment, and you **let it slip** when you say something you did not mean to say.

examples.text: He has been **let down** so many times in the past - I hope he won't be disappointed again.
Don't **let go of** the rope or she'll fall and hurt herself.
The accused was **let off** with a fine.
examples.note: received only a small punishment for a crime

examples.text: When she **let it slip** that she had been given a pay rise, the other workers were very angry.
examples.note: said it, sometimes without meaning to

lesson.heading: Break
lesson.text: You **break a promise** when you don't do what you said you would, and you **break a record** when you do better than anyone before you. **Break off** means to stop suddenly, and **break the news** means to tell someone something, usually something unwelcome.

examples.text: No one likes people who **break their promises**.
examples.note: don't do what they say they'll do

examples.text: The speaker **broke off** in the middle of a sentence.
I'm dreading **breaking the news** to him. He's going to be very upset.
When he left her, he **broke her heart**.
The sprinter **broke the record** for the 100 metres.
examples.note: ran faster than anyone had run before

lesson.text: Learn the whole expression, not the particle on its own: *run into a friend* and *run out of milk* share the verb but have nothing else in common.

exercises.prompt: Let's run ___ the plans for tomorrow's disco just once more.
exercises.explanation: Run over something = go through it quickly to check it.

exercises.prompt: First, I must see ___ the food arrangements.
exercises.explanation: See to / see about something = deal with it.

exercises.prompt: Make sure that none of the people who've said they'll help are going to break their ___.
exercises.explanation: To break a promise is to fail to do what you said you would do.

exercises.prompt: I don't imagine that many people will turn ___ until later.
Beata and Roshan said they'll come early and I'm sure they won't let us ___.
Match each expression with its meaning.

pairs.right: say something you didn't mean to say

exercises.prompt: I met Julio by chance at the station yesterday. Rewrite this using *run*.
options: I ran into Julio at the station yesterday.
I ran over Julio at the station yesterday.
I ran out of Julio at the station yesterday.
I ran off Julio at the station yesterday.
exercises.explanation: Run into someone = meet them by chance.

exercises.prompt: The police didn't charge the boy, only giving him a warning. Rewrite this using *let*.
options: The police let the boy off with a warning.
The police let the boy down with a warning.
The police let go of the boy with a warning.
The police let it slip to the boy with a warning.
exercises.explanation: Let someone off = give them only a small punishment, or none at all.

exercises.prompt: I thought I was ___ when I saw a monkey in the garden.
exercises.explanation: Be seeing things = imagine you can see something that isn't there.

exercises.prompt: My aunt ___ people who don't have a good job.
exercises.explanation: Look down on someone = despise them. The opposite is look up to.

exercises.prompt: Natalie has always ___ her older cousin.
exercises.explanation: Look up to someone = admire them.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order. (Dan has promised to improve his behaviour.)
exercises.answer: Dan has promised to turn over a new leaf.
exercises.explanation: Turn over a new leaf = start doing something in a better way.

exercises.statement: An enormous crowd turned down to hear the President speak.
exercises.explanation: It should be: An enormous crowd turned up to hear the President speak. Turn up = appear.

exercises.prompt: Which verb does each expression belong to?
